segments.title: A blockade force at Montevideo
segments.summary: Cumberland, Achilles, and Ajax probably gave the Royal Navy enough strength to contain Admiral Graf Spee off Montevideo, raising the question of what Force K was meant to do beyond blockade duty.
segments.body: The ships already off Montevideo appear sufficient for a heavy blockade. HMS Cumberland had joined HMS Achilles and HMS Ajax, and both the cruisers and Admiral Graf Spee had been battered. That force probably could have kept the German ship contained. Force K's rush south therefore points to a more demanding contingency than routine blockade duty.

evidence.note: Clarke weighs Cumberland, Achilles, and Ajax against the needs of a simple blockade.

segments.title: Renown closes the escape route
segments.summary: HMS Renown made an attempted breakout by Admiral Graf Spee far less likely to succeed, giving the cruiser cordon a fast battlecruiser backstop.
segments.body: An attempted breakout posed the obvious weakness in a cruiser blockade. HMS Renown was meant to close that route. After the damage already suffered, Admiral Graf Spee was unlikely to fight past a fast battlecruiser. Renown therefore turned a probable cordon into a much stronger trap.

evidence.note: Clarke says Renown would ensure the raider could not find a way out.

segments.title: Ark Royal and the Montevideo contingency
segments.summary: Ark Royal and the recently reconstructed Renown were too valuable for routine containment, suggesting that Force K was prepared to strike Admiral Graf Spee at sea or in Montevideo if Uruguay could not compel the ship to leave.
segments.body: Ark Royal was Britain's newest strike carrier, while Renown had emerged from reconstruction so extensive that calling it a refit understates the work. Committing both ships seems excessive for routine containment, especially in light of how the Royal Navy operated later in 1939. Force K appears to have been preparing for Uruguay to fail to enforce its will on Admiral Graf Spee, or for the German ship to head toward Argentina. Ark Royal's aircraft could then finish the operation at sea or in harbour. An attack in a neutral harbour would break the law, but the closing remark presents operational success as the Royal Navy's priority.

evidence.note: Clarke identifies Ark Royal as the newest strike carrier and Renown as recently reconstructed.
He links the force to a possible failure of Uruguayan control and an attack in harbour or at sea.
